newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S REMBRANDT CALLS ZUMA IRRESPONSIBLE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S REMBRANDT CALLS ZUMA IRRESPONSIBLE.

text.p: South Africa's Rembrandt Group criticised Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma in a full-page newspaper advert on Sunday, saying her recent remarks about the tobacco industry were unacceptable and irresponsible.

Zuma said in the Senate last week that tobacco companies were ignoring regulations on printing health warnings in their advertising and on cigarette packets. She warned the industry she might ban tobacco advertising altogether.
Johann Rupert, chairman of Rembrandt Group, said in what he called an open letter to Zuma on Sunday that those cigarette packs without health warnings found in South Africa had been smuggled in.
"On numerous occasions we have warned you and your colleagues that substantial increases in excise duty will result in increased cigarette smuggling," Rupert said.
"We warned you that you would find cheap smuggled cigarettes in the market, without health warnings...
"We warned that smuggling was out of control. Now that you have come to the same conclusion, you apparently accuse us of breaking the law," Rupert said.
He said law and order in South Africa was "in danger of total collapse" and said a cigarette smuggler could make 4,000 rand from a single car-load of cigarettes.
"It is ironic and sad that a company which dutifully pays its taxes and goes out of its way to comply with the letter and spirt of the law, is now being accused by you of breaking the law.
"We find the above situation totally unacceptable and irresponsible."

Referring to charges that health warnings could not be read on outdoor billboards carrying cigarette advertisements, Rupert said it would help if Zuma's colleagues in law enforcement caught the thieves who "routinely" stole the cables providing lighting for the billboards.
Zuma has been previously been at the centre of controversy over her decision to spend 14 million rand on a play intended to promote AIDS awareness.
At the time she was defended by President Nelson Mandela, who accused pharmaceutical companies of waging a smear campaign against her because they did not like her policies.
